For this year’s Big Game Pamphlet photo contest,
we asked participants to submit images that show
case the experience and traditions of hunting in
Washington. This is a pretty broad ask – and that
was exactly the point. We know that there are
so many unique and special traditions among
Washington hunters, whether you live and hunt
here or visit from out of state. We wanted to see
what makes hunting in Washington special to you!
Maybe you want to highlight the harvest from
your once-in-a-lifetime tag draw, or share a special
memory of taking your child hunting for the frst
time. Some of you are the frst to hit the woods on
opening day of archery season, while others may
go out several times through the fall to mentor
friends and family. Maybe your special hunting tra
dition is making that big game recipe your family
asks for every holiday! No matter your experience,
background, or pursuit, there is a place here for
Washington’s hunting opportunities are as di
verse as the hunters themselves. Residents and
visitors alike marvel at the broad range of eco
systems you can fnd in our state, from coastal
rainforests to high alpine meadows, sagebrush
steppe to rugged mountaintops. These varied
landscapes support all kinds of wild species, both

rare and common, and hunters’ contributions
support them all. Sustainable harvest promotes
healthy game populations, and funds generated
through hunting license sales and equipment ex
cise taxes help fund the Washington Department
of Fish and Wildlife’s (WDFW) conservation work
that supports Washington’s wildlife and people.

experiences for Washington hunters. I want to
highlight our MyWDFW app, an exciting new tool
for WDFW license holders. The new app supports
license purchases, displays active license privi
leges, and allows you to electronically tag your big
game harvest. I know we’re all big on traditions,

becoming a mobile license holder for the 2026

hunters have been asking for mobile licensing for
a long time, and I’m excited we are bringing this
update to Washington hunters this year.

145° F for whole meats, 160° F for ground meats, and 165° F for poultry.
